verdicts.dateTest: Claim: British American Tobacco p.l.c. held 22.91% of ITC through three vehicles on 31 Dec 2025. The cited ITC shareholding-pattern PDF is headed "Shareholding Pattern as on 31st December, 2025". So the date matches. The ownership window started earlier and is still open. ITC's Report and Accounts 2026 (Note on shareholders holding more than 5%) gives Tobacco Manufacturers (India) Ltd 2,54,14,95,863 shares (20.31%) at 31 Mar 2025, falling to 2,22,84,95,863 shares (17.79%) at 31 Mar 2026. That is the same share count as the Dec-2025 filing, so the 22.91% aggregate dates from BAT's May-2025 partial sale and was unchanged through 31 Mar 2026. No date conflict. The 'from' field of 2025-12-31 is the observation date, not the start of the holding.
verdicts.identityTest:
What the cited SHP shows, verified by curl plus pymupdf: Table III, "(2) Institutions (Foreign) (a) Foreign Direct Investment", 3 holders, 2,86,97,62,693 shares, 22.91% (22.78% on a fully diluted A+B+C2 basis). Named holders: "Tobacco Manufacturers (India) Limited 2,22,84,95,863 17.79"; "Myddleton Investment Company Limited 48,63,11,940 3.88"; "Rothmans International Enterprises Limited 15,49,54,890 1.24". The SHP also lists the three as persons acting in concert with each other.

What the SHP does NOT show: it never names British American Tobacco and never says 'wholly-owned'. The BAT attribution comes from other records:
(a) ITC Report and Accounts 2026 (https://www.itcportal.com/content/dam/itc-corporate/open-pdfs/report-and-accounts/ITC-Report-and-Accounts-2026.pdf): "He is a representative of Tobacco Manufacturers (India) Limited ('TMI'), a subsidiary of British American Tobacco p.l.c. ('BAT')". Related parties are listed as "Subsidiaries of British American Tobacco p.l.c. - of which the Company is an associate". Dividend payments went to TMI (Rs 3197.89 cr) and Myddleton (Rs 697.86 cr).
(b) UK Companies House: Myddleton Investment Company Ltd (00207434, registered at Globe House, 1 Water Street, London, BAT's head office) has a single PSC, Weston Investment Company Ltd, holding 75% or more. Rothmans International Enterprises Ltd (02694154, Globe House) has a single PSC, Rothmans International Ltd, holding 75% or more.
(c) TMI is not an Indian company despite its name. It is an overseas company incorporated in the Isle of Man (reg. 000512C; Companies House FC002714; UK establishment opened 1928).

So BAT control of all three vehicles is established. Exact 100% ('wholly-owned') ownership was not read in a primary document, because BAT's own annual report subsidiary list could not be fetched (bat.com returns 403).
verdicts.baseRate: In this file's own sample, 3 of the 6 companies checked have a foreign strategic or industrial holder with a stake of 1% or more (ITC/BAT, Bharti/Singtel-Pastel, Maruti/Suzuki). That is not discriminating, but it doesn't need to be: the claim asserts a fact, not impropriety, and says so. Foreign industrial legacy stakes of this kind are common in Indian large caps (colonial-era or JV parents: Suzuki, Unilever in HUL, Nestle, Siemens and others).
verdicts.denialFound: None needed and none found. The claim alleges no wrongdoing. BAT and ITC both disclose the stake themselves: ITC in its SHP and annual report, BAT by treating ITC as an associate. The parties were not asked. No contrary reporting found (web-search budget exhausted; checked through primary documents instead).
verdicts.innocentReading: This is the whole reading, not an alternative one. ITC began in 1910 as Imperial Tobacco Company of India, owned by BAT's predecessor. BAT kept a minority associate stake after Indianisation. It holds the stake through legacy UK and Isle of Man holding companies that it controls, and it appoints two non-executive directors to ITC's board (S. Panray and A. Singh, both "Representative of TMI as Investor"). The stake fell from about 25.4% to 22.91% when BAT sold part of it in May 2025. ITC reports "Shareholding of Promoters: Nil", so BAT is classified as a public institutional FDI holder, not a promoter.
verdicts.reason: The edge holds on the primary record. All three percentages, the 22.91% aggregate, the FDI category and the 31.12.2025 date match ITC's own SHP to the share. BAT control of the three vehicles is documented by ITC's audited Report and Accounts 2026 ("TMI, a subsidiary of British American Tobacco p.l.c."; related-party note naming BAT subsidiaries) and by Companies House PSC records. The claim-level text has one false statement. It calls BAT "the single largest named foreign shareholder found in this entire file", but the same file records Suzuki Motor Corp at about 58.65% of Maruti Suzuki (reported tier) and says outright that Suzuki exceeds BAT's 22.91%. Separately, 'wholly-owned' is stronger than any primary document actually read (PSC shows 75% or more; BAT's AR, which would state 100%, returned 403). Neither point breaks the edge s=cap:bat, t=co:itc, pred=own, d=22.91%. Both are wording fixes.

The NSE exchange API (corporate-share-holdings-master, symbol MARUTI) independently shows "date":"30-JUN-2026","pr_and_prgrp":"58.65","submissionDate":"17-JUL-2026". The 56.28% figure has a date after all: it is stale. Screener's own yearly table has Promoters at 56.28% for Mar 2020 only (56.21% 2017–19, 56.28% Mar 2020, 56.37% 2021–22, 56.48% 2023, 58.19% 2024, 58.28% 2025, 58.53% Mar 2026, 58.65% Jun 2026). So the 'About' text ("SMC currently holds 56.28% of its equity stake") is boilerplate from about March 2020 that was never updated. It is not a rival current figure.

verdicts.baseRate: Foreign parents holding majority promoter stakes in NIFTY 50 companies are rare: Maruti/SMC 58.65%, HUL/Unilever 61.90%, Nestle India/Nestle 62.76% (screener, Jun 2026). That is about 3 of 50 (≈6%), so the property does pick out a small group. However, "the largest single foreign shareholding" is true only inside this file's 15-company sample. Across the full NIFTY 50, Nestle's 62.76% of Nestle India and Unilever's 61.90% of HUL both exceed SMC's 58.65%. Neither company is covered in holders.json. The claim says "found in this file", which is literally accurate, but it will be misread as index-wide unless the scope is stated.
verdicts.denialFound: none found — not asked. None is needed: this is a disclosed, non-adverse ownership fact that Maruti and SMC state openly (SMC calls Maruti its largest subsidiary). No contra is required at reported tier.
verdicts.innocentReading: Nothing here is concealed and nothing needs explaining. Maruti began in 1982 as a Government of India–Suzuki JV. SMC became the majority owner in 2002, and its stake rose over time through ordinary corporate actions. The largest step, 56.48% to 58.19% in Dec 2023, matches the preferential allotment to SMC in the Suzuki Motor Gujarat buyout. The smaller rises in 2026 fit further SMC purchases or allotments. This is a foreign strategic promoter stake, legally disclosed each quarter under SEBI LODR Reg. 31.
verdicts.reason: The core fact survives. The 58.65% promoter-group holding at 30-Jun-2026 is confirmed by screener and independently by NSE's official shareholding API (filed 17-Jul-2026). The primary record I did open gives only the "promoter and promoter group" total.

verdicts.identityTest: Every identity matches. Downloaded 2026-09-26 and text-extracted. HDFC Bank: 'VANGUARD TOTAL INTERNATIONAL STOCK INDEX FUND AABTV0442N … 167330626 … 1.25' and 'VANGUARD EMERGING MARKETS STOCK INDEX FUND, A SERIES OF VANGUARD INTERNATIONAL EQUITY INDEX FUNDS AAATY0918K … 158405284 … 1.19'. That makes 2.44% combined, which matches. Also 'GOVERNMENT OF SINGAPORE AAAJG0594R … 2.17' and 'GOVERNMENT PENSION FUND GLOBAL AACCN1454E … 1.34'. Bharti Airtel: 'GOVERNMENT OF SINGAPORE … 1.22%' and 'GOVERNMENT PENSION FUND GLOBAL … 1.06%'. Neither names BlackRock or Vanguard. RIL: the FPI Category I line (16.52%) has no named sub-holder. ITC: the only named FPIs are 'GQG Partners Emerging Markets Equity Fund … 1.79' and 'Goldman Sachs Trust II - Goldman Sachs GQG Partners International Opportunities Fund … 1.42'. SBI: FPI Cat I is 9.37% with no named holder, and 'LIFE INSURANCE CORPORATION OF INDIA … 9.38'. A search of all five texts for blackrock, ishares, vanguard, fidelity, capital group, europacific, kuwait and abu dhabi finds Vanguard only in HDFC Bank and BlackRock/iShares nowhere. Identity rests on PAN-tagged fund names and NBIM's statutory fund name, not on a name match.
verdicts.baseRate: Same five-filing lens run on the comparison set: BlackRock 0/5, Vanguard 1/5 (HDFC Bank), NBIM/GPFG 2/5, GIC/Govt of Singapore 2/5, Capital Group, Fidelity, KIA and ADIA 0/5 each, and LIC (the domestic control) 4/5. BlackRock is therefore the least visible, not the most. The picture is graded, not uniformly alarming, and the lens does not manufacture the finding. The threshold is the weak point. SEBI's Reg 31 format names holders at ≥1% per registration (per PAN), and BlackRock and Vanguard split their holdings across many separately registered funds. So '0 of 5 named ≥1%' is a weak test of their combined stake. It rules out a single concentrated stake; it does not rule out a larger combined total. Rough scale check: the iShares MSCI India ETF reports net assets of '$6,019,525,338 as of Sep 25, 2026' (ishares.com INDA page). That is tiny next to an Indian listed market worth several trillion dollars. The sample is also not random: it is 5 of 50 constituents, chosen as the largest names.
verdicts.denialFound: None found; not asked. Neither BlackRock nor Vanguard was approached, and no statement from either on the 'own India' narrative is recorded. This matters less than usual: the narrative is rated unsupported, so it accuses no one of anything that needs a response. The absence should still be recorded as 'not asked'.
verdicts.innocentReading: Global index funds (MSCI EM/India, FTSE EM, total-international) must hold large Indian companies roughly in proportion to their index weight. Their stakes are minority, passive and spread across dozens of separately registered funds. Because of that split, each registration sits near or under the 1% naming line. Voting control stays with promoters (RIL, Airtel, ITC via BAT), the government (SBI) and domestic institutions such as LIC. Seen this way, the narrative mistakes AUM rankings and ETF index-tracking for ownership and control.
verdicts.reason: Every factual component checks out against the primary filings. BlackRock/iShares appears in none of the five as a named ≥1% holder. Vanguard appears only in HDFC Bank, through two funds (1.25% + 1.19% = 2.44%). The comparison set gives a graded, non-alarming picture. The one weakness is how much the 'unsupported' verdict leans on a ≥1% per-registration disclosure threshold that is built to miss holdings split across funds. That limits how strong the evidence is. It does not overturn the verdict: combined passive minority stakes do not meet any reading of 'own' or 'control', and the one scale figure checked (INDA about $6.0bn) supports that. The status should stay 'unsupported' (not 'debunked'), because combined BlackRock and Vanguard ownership was not measured. The counts are documented; the verdict is our own inference, so it is analytic.
verdicts.corrections: (1) Add the threshold caveat to the narrative text or strongestCounter: 'named ≥1%' is a per-registration SEBI Reg 31 disclosure line, BlackRock and Vanguard hold through many separately registered funds, and a 0/5 count limits single-vehicle concentration but does not measure combined ownership. The strongestCounter's 'not once' is accurate but reads as more than it proves. (2) Vanguard wording: say 'two separate Vanguard index funds each individually cross 1% in HDFC Bank (Total International Stock Index Fund 1.25%; Emerging Markets Stock Index Fund 1.19%; 2.44% combined, as of 30.06.2026)'. (3) Put the filing as-of dates in the narrative text (RIL and HDFC Jun-2026; ITC and Airtel Dec-2025; SBI Mar-2025) and flag SBI as stale. (4) State that the sample is 5 of 50 constituents and non-random (largest names). (5) Add a combined-scale datapoint to support the counter, e.g. iShares MSCI India ETF net assets US$6.02bn as of 2026-09-25 (https://www.ishares.com/us/products/239659/ishares-msci-india-etf), next to total Indian market capitalisation from an NSE or BSE source. Also add BlackRock and Vanguard 13F or N-PORT India totals to whatWouldChangeThis as the deciding fact. (6) Record 'BlackRock/Vanguard: not asked' as the response line. (7) Keep status 'unsupported'. Do not upgrade to 'debunked' until combined ownership is measured.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim restated: "Rothschild & Co (or any Rothschild-branded entity) holds or controls equity in Indian banks, as of the latest quarter." Evidence windows: the HDFC Bank SHP is as of 30.06.2026, which is current. The SBI SHP is as of 31.03.2025, about 18 months before asOf 2026-09-26, and a newer SBI filing exists but was not opened. The ICICI Bank figures are screener.in aggregates through Jun 2026. The windows overlap the claim's present tense closely enough, but SBI is stale and the narrative should say which date each check comes from. There is no chronology failure.
verdicts.identityTest: Mostly passes, with three defects. (1) The narrative gives the institution as "Rothschild & Co (Euronext: ROTH)". Rothschild & Co went private in 2023; the companion file mandates-ventures.json records it as "Euronext: ROTH, until 2023 delisting", and Wikipedia says the family announced in 2023 it would take the firm private. The current-listing identifier is stale. (2) The Indian entity is not identified in this file. It is identified elsewhere: CIN U65990MH1998PTC116788, SEBI Cat-I merchant banker INM000010668 (rothschildandco.com India page, opened). Reuse cap:rothschild-co / cap:rothschild-co-india. (3) "The Rothschilds" as a popular term also covers Edmond de Rothschild, a separate Swiss group with its own fund range, which sits outside the Rothschild & Co perimeter. Checking only Rothschild & Co leaves that name unexamined. This is immaterial at the ≥1% level, where neither name appears, but the identity scope should be stated.
verdicts.baseRate: Among foreign advisory firms, including the SPEC control Lazard as well as Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, JP Morgan and Citi at group level, the share appearing as a named ≥1% holder in the HDFC Bank or SBI SHP is 0 of 6 or more. Absence is therefore about 100% and does not single out Rothschild in either direction. The lens gives Lazard the same "absence" (mandates-ventures.json says so explicitly), so the result is a fact about advisory firms, not about Rothschild. The finding that actually discriminates lies elsewhere. In the two named-holder bank filings, the controlling holder is the Indian State: President of India 57.43% of SBI (SBI SHP 31.03.2025), with LIC at 9.38% of SBI and 4.77% of HDFC Bank. The largest foreign named holders of HDFC Bank are GIC/Government of Singapore (2.17%), Vanguard (two funds, 2.44% combined) and NBIM/GPFG (1.34%). The denominator is thin: 2 named-holder bank filings out of about 12 listed PSBs and about 21 listed private banks. Publish that denominator.
verdicts.denialFound: None found. Rothschild & Co was not asked, and no response is needed because the narrative accuses no documented act by the firm. The firm's own India page (https://www.rothschildandco.com/en/countries/india/) describes its business as "M&A and Strategic Advisory, Global Markets Solutions including fundraising and strategic capital, and Global Financing Solutions and Restructuring & Liability Management". It mentions no banking licence or bank equity stakes. That is a self-description, not a denial.
verdicts.innocentReading: The boring explanation fits completely. Rothschild & Co India is a Mumbai merchant-banking and advisory subsidiary of about 30 bankers that earns deal fees. Indian banks' equity is held by the State (the President of India controls SBI and the other PSBs), by LIC and domestic mutual funds, and by fragmented foreign portfolio investors led by sovereign and index funds (GIC, NBIM, Vanguard). The surname persists as shorthand because of 19th-century banking history (Ferguson), not because of any current Indian shareholding.
verdicts.reason:
The verdict "unsupported" survives. No source shows any Rothschild entity holding Indian bank equity, and the two primary filings opened show the Indian State (57.43% of SBI) and LIC as controlling or major holders. That is a stronger counter than the one the file gives. The supporting prose, however, contains three factual defects that must be fixed before publication.

(a) Overclaim on threshold. The strongestCounter says "not ≥1%, not at any threshold". Both cited SEBI filings state: "The above format needs to disclose name of all holders holding more than 1% of total number of shares." Absence below 1% therefore cannot be established from these sources.

(b) Wrong source count and misused evidence. It says "5 NIFTY 50 companies' shareholding patterns checked, including three of India's largest listed banks". The five named-holder filings include only two banks, HDFC Bank and SBI. ICICI Bank comes only from screener.in aggregates (FIIs 33.79%, DIIs 42.32% at Jun 2026). Those aggregates name no holder, so they cannot evidence the absence of any named holder.

(c) Stale identifier. "Euronext: ROTH" is given as current, but the firm delisted in 2023.

The advisory characterisation is correct but is unsourced in this file. The narrative is a family-as-actor claim, so it must never become an edge. It stays a narrative, rated unsupported, resting on our analytic reading of documented filings.

verdicts.dateTest: As a sentence: SEBI issued a granular FPI beneficial-ownership disclosure circular in August 2023, after Hindenburg's report of 24 January 2023. The order of events holds. The one cited source, TaxGuru (Dev Agarwal, published 23 Sep 2025), says "SEBI rolled out new disclosure norms on 10 August 2023, with phased enforcement beginning 1 November." The entity record (cap:sebi-fpi-disclosure-2023) and the companion file (rules-regulators:c019, from 2023-08-24) date the circular 24 August 2023. So the record has two different dates for the same rule, and the text should use the circular date, 24 Aug 2023. The bigger date problem is that the claim describes the 2023 rule as if it still applies. By this file's asOf date (2026-09-26), SEBI's 209th board meeting (24 Mar 2025) had doubled the size threshold from Rs 25,000 cr to Rs 50,000 cr. That change is recorded in rules-regulators:c020, which supersedes c019. There were also carve-outs for no-identified-promoter companies (Mar 2024) and university funds (Aug 2024). And the Adani matter itself moved on: SC expert committee (May 2023), SC judgment (Jan 2024), SEBI's final Adani orders (Sep 2025). The narrative mentions none of these.
verdicts.identityTest: The list "every named ≥1% holder this file actually found (NBIM, GIC, Vanguard, GQG, Google, BAT)" is incomplete. The file's own claim holders:c014 records Pastel Limited, a Mauritius-incorporated vehicle, holding 7.49% of Bharti Airtel as a foreign promoter-group holder. That is the largest foreign line in that filing, and it is the only ≥1% holder in the sample domiciled in the jurisdiction the round-tripping narrative is about. Pastel is Singtel's disclosed vehicle, so the transparency conclusion survives, but leaving it out of a list headed "every" is wrong. The list also mixes categories. BAT's 22.91% is Foreign Direct Investment, not FPI, and Pastel is promoter-group, so neither tests a claim about "FPI money". In the record's strongestCounter, GQG is described as an "index-fund family"; it is an active emerging-markets manager, and it is also the best-known post-Hindenburg buyer of Adani shares. GIC is said to "publish" its holdings; GIC does not publish a holdings list. It appears in these filings only as the named FPI 'GOVERNMENT OF SINGAPORE'. Named sovereigns are transparent on beneficial ownership, but not because they publish holdings, and sovereign/government Category I FPIs were exempt from the size-based granular disclosure in the first place.
verdicts.baseRate: The test used, "named ≥1% holders are transparent", does not discriminate. In a NIFTY 50 company outside the Adani group, a 1% stake is worth thousands of crores, so almost every such named holder is a sovereign, a large regulated fund family or a strategic corporate. In this sample it was 100%, well past the 80% line. Where the narrative actually applies, the figure is different. Hindenburg's own report (hindenburgresearch.com/adani/) found opaque Mauritius FPIs named at ≥1% in Adani company filings: APMS Investment Fund 2.26%, Albula 2.43%, Cresta 2.30%, LTS 1.54% and Elara India Opportunities 3.91% of Adani Green (June 2019), and Lotus Global 4.51% of Adani Enterprises (Dec 2008). Two NIFTY 50 constituents, Adani Enterprises (co:adani-enterprises) and Adani Ports (co:adani-ports), are in research/raw/indices.json, but neither was among the five filings opened. The sample left out the only index members where this lens could tell anything apart.
verdicts.denialFound: None is recorded in this file, and the narrative carries no contra. Records elsewhere in the repository: the SC-appointed expert committee (reported 6 May 2023) found prima facie no regulatory failure and called SEBI's search for the ultimate owners of 13 Adani-linked FPIs potentially "a journey without a destination" (research/raw/capital/rules-regulators.json, rules-regulators:c023, via LiveLaw https://www.livelaw.in/top-stories/supreme-court-sc-adani-hindenburg-report-expert-committee-securities-and-exchange-board-of-india-sebi-regulatory-failure-229112). SEBI's September 2025 final orders dismissed Hindenburg's related-party allegations (cited in that file as atlas energy:doc-sebi-adani-orders-2025). verdicts.dateTest: Written as: BJP (Sambit Patra at a party media briefing, plus the BJP's X account) accused OCCRP of being a US State Department / "deep state" media tool meant to destabilise India by targeting Modi, on Thursday 5 Dec 2024. ThePrint (Sakshi Dayal and YP Rajesh, 07 Dec 2024, 01:48 pm IST) says Patra spoke "at an official media briefing by the party on Thursday", which was 5 Dec 2024. The claim's "7 Dec 2024" and from=2024-12-07 are the article's publication date, not the date of the statement. This is a two-day error that can be fixed. Order of events: Mediapart/Drop Site report on OCCRP funding (early Dec 2024), US indictment of Adani (Nov 2024), BJP accusation (5 Dec). The accusation came after the facts it cites, so no chronology problem.
verdicts.identityTest: The node s=bjp is correct: the party is the actor. The label misattributes one quote, though. The only words ThePrint gives to Patra personally are: "A French investigative media group…has revealed that… 50% of OCCRP's funding comes directly from the U.S. State Department. OCCRP has served as a media tool for carrying out a deep state agenda." The phrase "The Deep State had a clear objective to destabilise India by targeting Prime Minister Modi" is attributed to "the BJP said in a series of messages on X", not to Patra. The 'd' field names "Mediapart", but ThePrint only says "a French investigative media group"/"a French media report". Naming Mediapart is our own inference (probably correct, since Mediapart co-published with Drop Site), but the cited source does not say it. The target t=energy:occrp is the right entity. Predicate: CONTRACT defines `enforce` as "agency → subject: cancellation, suspension, freeze, investigation, sanction, debarment". The BJP is a political party, not an agency, and a press-briefing accusation is none of those actions. So the predicate is wrong under the contract, even though the file uses `enforce` for several party accusations (bjp, energy:inc).
verdicts.baseRate: This does not discriminate as evidence about OCCRP. Governing parties calling foreign-funded investigative outlets a "foreign hand" or "deep state" tool is common across regimes (Fidesz on OSF, Russia's "foreign agent" labels, and Indian governments of both parties since Indira Gandhi's "foreign hand" rhetoric). OCCRP's large US-government funding share is openly disclosed and applies to all of its reporting worldwide, not just India. So the funding fact cannot single out the Adani reporting as directed. Symmetry check: the same lens would read any OCCRP story about an opposition-linked or rival-country figure as US-directed too, which shows the lens does no work. As a record of what the party said, the edge is accurate and discriminating: the BJP actually said it.
verdicts.denialFound: Yes, in the same article (ThePrint, 7 Dec 2024, https://theprint.in/diplomacy/attempt-to-destabilise-india-bjp-claims-us-state-dept-targeting-country-with-adani-indictment/2392501/). OCCRP: "The U.S. government, while providing some funding to OCCRP, has no say in our editorial processes." US State Department spokesperson: support for journalists "does not influence the editorial decisions or direction of these organizations" and "It's disappointing that the ruling party in India would make these kinds of accusations." Congress and Soros were asked and "did not immediately respond". Hindenburg is not mentioned in the article, so there is no record that it was asked or that it responded.
verdicts.innocentReading: OCCRP does get a large share of its budget from US-government grants. OCCRP says so itself, and the French report the BJP cited confirms it. But it is a pan-regional nonprofit newsroom with many donors, and funding at that level does not show editorial direction of any particular story. The Nov 2024 US indictment of Adani was brought by DOJ/SEC through court process, separate from OCCRP's Aug 2023 reporting. Linking the two is the BJP's inference. The simpler reading is a governing party answering damaging coverage of an allied business group with a foreign-interference frame, as is common.
verdicts.reason: The central record holds: ThePrint, a credible outlet with named sourcing, reports the BJP (Patra at a media briefing plus the party's X posts) calling OCCRP a US State Department "deep state" media tool meant to destabilise India by targeting Modi. As a narrative edge recording what the party said, it survives, and `alleged` is the right tier for its content. It has a real documented contra (c021: OCCRP and the State Department, same article). What does not survive: the statement date (5 Dec, not 7 Dec), the attribution of the "destabilise India by targeting PM Modi" quote to Patra (it came from the BJP's X posts), the "Mediapart" name (not in the source), the `enforce` predicate (the BJP is not an agency and took no enforcement action), and c038 listed as a contra (Hindenburg was not addressed, has no source and made no denial, so it cannot count as a contra). verdicts.dateTest: Written out, the claim is: SEBI, in its January 2018 board decision ("Easing of Access Norms for FPIs"), removed the 20-investor broad-based floor, and this structurally benefited concentrated FPIs holding Adani shares, 2018-2023. The premise is false as stated. The board paper at https://www.sebi.gov.in/sebi_data/meetingfiles/jan-2018/1515989011412_1.pdf keeps the definition: a broad-based fund "has at least twenty investors, with no investor holding more than 49%". Para 3.2.4 only extends the existing "deemed to be broad based" treatment. Until then it applied only to funds with a bank investor. The paper widens it to "Sovereign Wealth Fund, Insurance/ Reinsurance Companies, Pension Funds, Exchange Traded Funds". Para 3.2.14 adds a 3-month cure period for a fund that "due to exit of some offshore global investors loses its broad based status". The broad-based condition for Category II was dropped only by the SEBI (FPI) Regulations 2019 (September 2019). The proposals were sent to DEA, DoR and RBI on 24 May 2017, well before the January 2023 Hindenburg report.
verdicts.identityTest: Fails. The claim names the wrong rule. The "2018 amendment" that the SC expert committee, the petitioners and the Supreme Court discussed was the beneficial-owner / "opaque structures" amendment, not the broad-based investor floor. SC judgment of 3 January 2024 (Vishal Tiwari v UoI, para 20, hosted at https://www.sebi.gov.in/sebi_data/attachdocs/jan-2024/1704888578340.pdf): "These requirements were amended by SEBI in 2018 and 2019 by removing the requirement of disclosing ownership of the FPIs by a natural person." Para 26: "The 2018 amendment required mandatory disclosures by all FPIs ... It marked a shift towards tightening ... provisions on 'opaque structures' being omitted in 2019." The broad-based rule is not mentioned anywhere in the judgment. The node cap:sebi-fpi-2018-broadbased-amendment mixes up two different rule changes.
verdicts.baseRate: Non-discriminating. The deemed-broad-based extension and the 3-month cure period apply to every Category II fund that has sovereign-wealth, pension, insurer or ETF investors, and that is most of the institutional FPI universe (by count and by AUM, easily over 80%). The change was industry-wide market-access relief, sent to DEA, DoR and RBI in May 2017, with no issuer-specific element. Symmetry: the same lens would tie the 2018 easing to every group with concentrated FPI holders, so it picks out nothing specific to Adani.
verdicts.denialFound: SEBI's position, recorded in the SC judgment of 3 January 2024 (paras 25-27, at https://www.sebi.gov.in/sebi_data/attachdocs/jan-2024/1704888578340.pdf): the 2018 amendment "marked a shift towards tightening", and SEBI "claims no disability in its investigation into the Adani group on account of the amendments to the FPI Regulations". SEBI also said the expert committee mistook its use of the word "opaque". The Court held that "The FPI Regulations and LODR Regulations have been tightened by the amendments in question" and refused to order them revoked. The Adani Group rejected the Hindenburg allegations in its 413-page reply, as noted in the LiveLaw source. No party was asked about the broad-based framing specifically; none found, not asked.
verdicts.innocentReading: The January 2018 changes were routine market-access relief. Investor counts in open-ended funds rise and fall, and institutional investors such as SWFs, pension funds and insurers are already regulated. So SEBI treated them like banks when deciding whether a fund is broad-based, and gave funds a cure period instead of automatic reclassification. It was proposed in 2017, long before any Adani allegation. The broad-based label is a registration category, not a beneficial-ownership rule: UBO disclosure under PMLA Rule 9 applied either way.
verdicts.reason: This is decisive on two counts. (1) The Jan 2018 SEBI board paper did not remove the 20-investor floor; it kept that definition and only extended deemed-broad-based status plus added a cure period. (2) The only cited source, LiveLaw of 19 May 2023, never mentions broad-based funds, the 20-investor rule or any 2018 amendment. The primary court record shows that the 2018 amendment at issue was the UBO/opaque-structure change, which SEBI and the Supreme Court call a tightening. Neither the expert committee nor Hindenburg is shown pointing to the broad-based floor. The benefit to grp:adani therefore rests on a mistaken rule and on sources that do not say what the claim says. An "analytic" tier cannot cover a false factual premise.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim as written: "ICEA/IESA lobbied → DPIIT eased PN3 via Press Note 2, March 2026". The only source is a BDO India page reposting The Telegraph, published 12 March 2026. It dates the Cabinet approval to "Tuesday", which is 10 March 2026. The ICEA and IESA quotes are reactions given after that decision, not lobbying before it. The page also says pending applications "will go through the automatic route once the notification is issued", so as of 12 March no notification had been issued. Nothing in the file sources the record's 15 March 2026 notification date or the name "Press Note 2 (2026)". The source gives neither the press-note number nor a notification date. The DPIIT press-notes page loaded but returned no readable 2026 listing (it appears to render with JavaScript). So the event is dated to March 2026 by Cabinet approval, but the number and the 15 March date are unverified. The ordering "after lobbying support" is not shown: the source's timeline has the endorsement coming after the decision.
verdicts.identityTest: The two industry bodies are named correctly. Pankaj Mohindroo is described as "chairman of the India Cellular and Electronics Association", but the record calls him "president", which is wrong. Ashok Chandak as "president of the India Electronics and Semiconductor Association" is correct. The claim tags IESA/ICEA as "electronics/solar PLI manufacturers dependent on Chinese suppliers". The source does not say this. Neither body is a solar association: IESA covers semiconductors and electronics, and ICEA covers mobile phones and electronics. The source mentions ECMS, not PLI, and never mentions dependence on Chinese suppliers. The target node "cap:land-border-investors" is also wrong in substance. According to the source, the relaxation does not cover direct investment by land-border-country investors. DPIIT JS Jai Prakash Shivahare: "All the restrictions for investors from LBCs are still applicable. This relaxation is only for entities in non-LBCs and having beneficial owners from LBCs below 10 per cent and non-controlling stake."
verdicts.baseRate: Industry bodies publicly welcoming a reform that affects their sector is close to universal. Nearly every FDI easing draws favourable quotes from the relevant associations (CII, FICCI, NASSCOM, ICEA and others), so this is non-discriminating (above 80%). A welcome quote after the fact tells us nothing about who asked for the change. The source's own stated driver is structural: about 600 applications had piled up under PN3.
verdicts.denialFound: none found, not asked. There is nothing to deny because the source makes no lobbying allegation. Government's stated rationale, in the BDO/Telegraph piece: the backlog of about 600 pending applications, ease of doing business and manufacturing investment. DPIIT Secretary Amardeep Singh Bhatia and JS Shivahare are quoted (https://www.bdo.in/en-gb/news/2026/india-eases-fdi-rules-under-press-note-3-with-10-per-cent-cap-for-border-country-investors).
verdicts.innocentReading: From 2020 the blanket approval requirement in PN3 also caught global funds and non-LBC entities with small Chinese or Hong Kong LPs or shareholders, and about 600 applications piled up. The government created a 10% non-controlling beneficial-ownership threshold for those non-LBC entities, plus a 60-day track for named manufacturing sectors. Electronics associations welcomed it afterwards, as associations routinely do. Chandak's quote is specifically about "global fund participation", which fits the indirect-beneficial-ownership fix, not Chinese strategic capital.
verdicts.reason: The claim's causal part ("after lobbying support from ICEA and IESA") is not in the only cited source. The source shows the two bodies welcoming the change after the Cabinet decision, which is a reaction, not a request. The claim also misstates the rule. It does not let "land-border-country (incl. China) investors" take automatic-route stakes of up to 10%. It lets non-LBC entities whose LBC beneficial owners hold under 10%, non-controlling, use the automatic route, and DPIIT says all restrictions on LBC investors themselves remain. The "solar", "PLI" and "dependent on Chinese suppliers" descriptors are the author's own additions. The record's tier is "documented", but it rests on a single secondary source: a consulting firm reposting a Telegraph article, with a BDO partner quoted, which gives BDO a self-interest. That is at most "reported" until the DPIIT press note or a PIB release is attached.
verdicts.corrections: 1) Remove "after lobbying support from ICEA and IESA". Replace it with "welcomed after Cabinet approval by ICEA chairman Pankaj Mohindroo and IESA president Ashok Chandak". Change "president" to "chairman" for Mohindroo in entity cap:press-note-2026-easing d[1] and in the claim's d[0]. 2) Rewrite the rule: "non-LBC investing entities with LBC beneficial ownership below 10% and non-controlling may use the automatic route; direct LBC investment still requires government approval; 60-day expedited approval for capital goods, electronic capital goods, electronic components, polysilicon, ingot-wafer." 3) Remove "solar", "PLI" and "dependent on Chinese suppliers". The source mentions none of them (it cites ECMS, raised to ₹40,000 crore), and neither body is a solar association. 4) Change the tier from "documented" to "reported" (one secondary outlet, The Telegraph via BDO, 12 March 2026). To upgrade to documented, attach the DPIIT press note PDF or the PIB Cabinet release. 5) Change "from" from 2026-03-15 to 2026-03-10 (Cabinet approval), unless the notification date is sourced. The "Press Note 2 (2026)" number and the 15 March date are currently unsourced, so either source them or mark them unverified. 6) Reconsider the target node. Better targets are "non-LBC entities with minority LBC beneficial owners" and "global funds with LBC LPs"; cap:land-border-investors as currently written fits poorly. 7) Add the stated driver, "~600 pending applications backlog", as the who-asked or why field required by the SPEC's rule-change control, and add a symmetry note that PN3 (2020) and this easing both came under the same NDA government.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim: SEBI (board, 209th meeting, chaired by Tuhin Kanta Pandey, who took charge 1 March 2025) raised the FPI size-based granular-disclosure threshold on 24 March 2025. Tenure overlaps. BusinessToday is dated 24 March 2025 and says the change was "announced" that day, without separately dating the board meeting. Business Upturn says "its 209th board meeting held in Mumbai" (published 24 March 2025, updated 14 July 2026). The date passes, but it rests on the press, not the SEBI press release, which I could not reach (the SEBI listing and a guessed URL returned nothing or 404).
verdicts.identityTest: The actor is SEBI (the board), and the subject is FPIs with Indian equity AUM above the threshold. Both sources name the same body and the same instrument (the Aug 2023 additional-disclosure framework for FPIs). There is no identity mismatch. The "Adani-linked FPIs" in the claim are not named or identified in either source.
verdicts.baseRate: This is a rule of general application covering every FPI above the size threshold, so it does not single out any holder or group. Its rationale is scale-driven: BT says "The average trading volume in the cash market has increased by 122 per cent." It supports no inference about who benefited apart from large diversified FPIs in general. Symmetry check under the SPEC's rule-change control: the tightening (Aug 2023, after Hindenburg) and the easing (Mar 2025) both happened under the same NDA-era regulator. No record in the file names who asked for the change. The file already logs that as a gap.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable in the usual sense, since this is a regulatory decision, not an allegation. SEBI's own stated reason is the response on record: the size criterion is being indexed to market growth (cash volumes up 122%), and "no changes are being made to the 50% group-level concentration threshold" (Business Upturn). No one was asked about the "caught the Adani-linked FPIs" framing, and neither source makes that link.
verdicts.innocentReading: A fixed rupee threshold set in 2023 was catching more diversified FPIs each year simply because the market grew. SEBI indexed it upward and explicitly kept the group-concentration test aimed at promoter-linked structuring ("prevent any structuring that could potentially bypass key regulatory guardrails—especially in cases where FPIs are used as vehicles for concentrated promoter interests"). This reads as routine recalibration, not a loosening aimed at any group.
verdicts.reason: The core facts are confirmed by two outlets. BusinessToday: "raise the threshold limit for foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) from the present Rs 25,000 crore of equity AUM" to "FPIs holding more than Rs 50,000 crore of equity AUM ... will now be required to make additional disclosures". Business Upturn: "double the threshold for size-based FPI disclosures from ₹25,000 crore to ₹50,000 crore" and "no changes are being made to the 50% group-level concentration threshold". The claim survives on that. What neither source says is the clause "that caught the Adani-linked FPIs". Neither article mentions Adani; in BT, Adani appears only in unrelated ads on the page. Whether the 50% test actually "caught" Adani-linked FPIs, rather than being designed with them in mind (some funds may have rebalanced to avoid it), is a separate factual claim that needs its own source. "Reducing the number of FPIs required to disclose" is a fair logical consequence, but neither source gives a count. Business Upturn is a thin outlet, and the SEBI board press release, the primary record, is not cited. So the tier holds at reported, not documented. The file record currently says "documented".
verdicts.corrections: 1. The file record's tier ("documented") conflicts with the claim's tier ("reported"). Set it to reported until the SEBI 24 Mar 2025 board-meeting press release (209th meeting) is added as a source. Documented is justified only with that primary source. 2. Reword the Adani clause, both in the text and in d[0] ("the one that actually caught the Adani-linked FPIs"). Use "retaining the 50%-single-corporate-group concentration test introduced in Aug 2023 after the Hindenburg–Adani episode", and cite the SEBI circular of 24 Aug 2023. Alternatively, add a source showing named Adani-linked FPIs were in fact made to disclose under that test; without one, drop "caught". 3. Qualify "reducing the number of FPIs required to disclose" as an inference, or cite a count. 4. Add "209th board meeting" to the record's d field for identity. 5. Keep the "who asked" gap as recorded.

verdicts.identityTest: The actor is SEBI and the instrument is circular SEBI/HO/AFD/AFD-POD-2/P/CIR/2024/104 (EY footnote 2). The governed class is university funds and university-related endowments that are registered, or eligible to register, as Category I FPIs. They sit inside cap:fpi-industry, so s->t direction and node choice are correct for a `law` edge. No person, family or ethnic group is framed as the actor.
verdicts.baseRate: Mostly not applicable. This is a regulatory-fact edge, not an inference from a shared property. The August 2023 framework already carved out several classes of FPI (government and government-related entities, and certain listed or regulated pooled vehicles). Adding one more named, conditional class is routine regulatory calibration. On its own it does not point to targeted favouritism. The 25%-of-global-AUM cap keeps out any fund whose book is concentrated in India.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable: there is no accusation to deny. SEBI's stated rationale, via EY, is "enhancing the ease of doing business in India for FPIs", and the exemption was "based on feedback received" on the 27 Feb 2024 consultation paper. None found; SEBI not asked.
verdicts.innocentReading: The boring reading fits. University endowments are large, diversified, tax-exempt non-profits that are hard-pressed to look through to natural persons. SEBI consulted publicly in Feb 2024 and exempted them in Aug 2024 under hard conditions (India equity AUM under 25% of global AUM, global AUM over INR 100 bn, proof of tax-exempt non-profit status, domicile in an eligible jurisdiction). The concentration test that caught the Adani-linked FPIs stays in force for everyone else.
verdicts.reason: The only cited source (EY Regulatory Alert, 06 Aug 2024, PDF at ey.com/content/dam/.../additional-disclosure-framework-for-foreign-portfolio-investors-sebi-consultation-paper.pdf) states the claim nearly word for word. It gives the date, actor, circular number, the exempted class, "subject to compliance with certain conditions", and the three conditions listed on the node. The claim text is a neutral statement of a regulatory fact. It passes. The tier is right at `reported`: one credible professional-services outlet citing the named circular. I could not reach the SEBI primary; two guessed sebi.gov.in URLs returned 404 and the circular listing page returned nothing on universities. The claim can move to `documented` once the SEBI circular itself (SEBI/HO/AFD/AFD-POD-2/P/CIR/2024/104) is cited.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim is: Hindenburg alleged on 10 Aug 2024 that the Buchs held a stake in IPE Plus Fund 1, made in 2015. That checks out. The archived Hindenburg report (web.archive.org of hindenburgresearch.com/sebi-chair-conflicts/) says "Published on August 10, 2024" and "Madhabi Buch and her husband Dhaval Buch first appear to have opened their account with IPE Plus Fund 1 on June 5th, 2015 in Singapore". She became a SEBI whole-time member in April 2017 and Chairperson in March 2022. The holding window per Hindenburg runs from 5 Jun 2015 through at least the 26 Feb 2018 account statement. The redemption request was sent 25 Feb 2018, which is during her WTM tenure. So the stake predates her appointment but also overlaps about 10 months of her time as a whole-time member. The record's d says only "The investment predates both her 2017 appointment", which leaves out that overlap. There is also a date error on the edge: it is an `own` edge with from=2024-08-10 and to=null, which reads as ownership starting in 2024 and still ongoing. The ownership window is 2015-06-05 to about 2018. 2024-08-10 is the date of the allegation, not of the ownership.
verdicts.identityTest: The person is right: Madhabi Puri Buch, SEBI Chairperson Mar 2022 to Feb 2025, with spouse Dhaval Buch. The fund is right: Hindenburg names it "GDOF Cell 90 (IPEplus Fund 1)", a Mauritius-registered cell below the Bermuda Global Dynamic Opportunities Fund, managed by IIFL (now 360 ONE). No LEI, CIN or registration number is recorded for the fund node, and none is available from these sources. The phrase "tied to a Vinod Adani associate" misstates what Hindenburg said. The report says a "Vinod Adani controlled company had invested in GDOF ... which then invested in IPE Plus Fund 1", meaning Vinod Adani himself used the structure. It says the fund's founder and CIO, Anil Ahuja, "was a director of Adani Enterprises ... three terms spanning nine years ending in June 2017". Its summary line is "run by an Adani director and significantly used by Vinod Adani".
verdicts.baseRate: Not computable. There is no public dataset of SEBI members' pre-appointment offshore holdings. As the file's own void notes, no public recusal or conflict-of-interest register existed before the 2025 High-Level Committee. What would make the claim stand out is that the fund was small (US$38.43m AUM at Dec 2017, per Hindenburg citing IIFL) and shared a structure with a Vinod Adani entity. That cannot be benchmarked against other regulators' holdings. Symmetry: an identical fields check on other SEBI members or earlier chairs is impossible for the same reason (no register). verdicts.innocentReading: A couple of private citizens living in Singapore in 2015 invested salary money in a small IIFL-managed offshore fund because its CIO was a family friend. They did this two years before she held any regulatory office. The fund's other investors, including a Vinod Adani entity, had nothing to do with their choice. Required disclosures were made to SEBI on appointment, and the units were redeemed in 2018. Under this reading, sharing a fund vehicle with Vinod Adani's entity is a coincidence of the same manager and structure, not a conflict. It stays open whether any recusal on Adani matters followed, because no recusal log has been published.
verdicts.reason: The core claim holds against the primary document. The archived Hindenburg report of 10 Aug 2024 does allege "hidden stakes" in IPE Plus Fund 1, with the account opened on 5 Jun 2015, so "alleged" is the right tier for the "undisclosed" part. The Buchs' own statement admits the 2015 investment, so the existence of the holding is effectively conceded. It is the "hidden/undisclosed" part and the alleged conflict that remain disputed. The claim is not refuted, but the record has specific errors. (1) The only cited source (NewsOnAir) says just "owned stakes in offshore entities linked to the Adani Group" and 2015. It does not name IPE Plus Fund 1, Mauritius or Vinod Adani, so the source check is partial and the primary report must be added. (2) "Vinod Adani associate" misstates the allegation: Hindenburg says Vinod Adani himself used the structure and the fund was run by an Adani director (Anil Ahuja). (3) The record's d says the stake size was not stated in the report, which is false: Hindenburg gives US$872,762.25 per a 26 Feb 2018 account statement. (4) The own-edge dates show the allegation date, not the ownership window. (5) supersededBy c028 is wrong, because the Lokpal dismissal of corruption complaints does not supersede the allegation that the stake existed.
